v.why: Removing the input-to-output skip residual hurts far more than removing a conv or pool on that edge (exp 1 vs 2, 3).
Filling an empty input-to-output edge restores a direct path and gives large gains (exp 71, 75-79).
Replacing the residual skip on edge 3 with a 1x1 conv loses the identity shortcut (exp 72).
With edge 4 absent, removing edge 3 leaves only one path to the output, which is much more damaging (exp 4, 6).
Removing edge 5 when edge 4 is already gone strips most of the computation reaching the output (exp 63, 64).
Adding a skip into the output helps most when the main input-to-output residual is missing (exp 34).
A skip on edge 1 supplies an identity path that substitutes for a missing edge-3 residual (exp 57, 58).
Skips on both edge 0 and edge 4 create a redundant identity path parallel to edge 3 and remove conv depth (exp 37).
When edge 2 is none, node 1 feeds the output only via edge 4, so a conv on edge 0 adds less (exp 25, 27).
In skip-heavy cells with little conv capacity, adding a 3x3 conv on the final edge gives large gains (exp 16, 19).

raw:
Ten hypotheses, each grounded in the 100 experiments and in how this cell is wired:

- **Edge 3 (input → output) is the main residual path.**
  - Deleting it costs far more when it is a skip_connect (#1 vs #2).
  - Filling it when it is empty is strongly positive (#71, #75–79).
  - Replacing a skip there with a 1×1 conv hurts (#72).
- **Removing the last remaining paths to the output is catastrophic.** Deleting edge 3 or edge 5 is much worse when edge 4 is already none (#4, #6, #63, #64).
- **Adding a skip_connect where none exists helps.**
  - A skip on edge 4 or edge 1 helps most when edge 3 is none (#34, #57, #58).
  - A skip on edge 4 hurts when edge 0 is already a skip, because the two skips in series duplicate the edge 3 shortcut (#37).
- **A conv on edge 0 is worth less when edge 2 is none.** Node 1 then reaches the output only through edge 4 (#25, #27).
- **A conv on edge 5 is worth more in skip-heavy cells** that otherwise have little conv capacity (#16, #19).

Several of these rest on one or two experiments, so the evidence for #4, #8, #9 and #10 in the list below is thin.
